subject: Computer Networking
title: The Browser Wars
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Browser Wars.

hook.text: Netscape Navigator vs. Internet Explorer. The battle for the browser defined the mid-1990s tech landscape.

buildup.text: Netscape launched in 1994 and dominated quickly. Microsoft bundled IE with Windows in 1995 to compete.

discovery.text: Both browsers added features at breakneck speed — JavaScript, CSS, plugins — often incompatibly.

twist.text: Microsoft's bundling strategy worked. IE reached 95% market share by 2002. Netscape collapsed.

climax.text: Netscape open-sourced its code before dying. That code became Firefox, which reignited browser competition.

punchline.text: Netscape lost the war but lit the spark for open-source browsers.

quiz.question: What happened to Netscape's code after the company declined?
options: It was open-sourced and became the basis for Firefox
It was sold to Apple for Safari

details.summary: The browser wars of the mid-1990s pitted Netscape Navigator against Microsoft's Internet Explorer. Microsoft bundled IE with Windows, gaining dominant market share. The competition drove rapid innovation but also produced incompatible web standards.
details.whyItMatters: The browser wars shaped the modern web by driving innovation while demonstrating the danger of platform lock-in. They also demonstrated that distribution bundling can defeat superior technology.
takeaways: Netscape and Internet Explorer competed for browser dominance
Microsoft bundled IE with Windows to gain market share
The conflict drove both innovation and standards fragmentation

faq.question: How did Microsoft win the first browser war?
faq.answer: Microsoft bundled Internet Explorer free with Windows, which was installed on most PCs. Netscape charged for its browser. Distribution advantage overwhelmed product quality. IE's market share rose from single digits to over 95 percent by 2002.

faq.question: What was the lasting impact of the browser wars?
faq.answer: Netscape released its code as open source, which became Mozilla Firefox. The W3C strengthened web standards to prevent vendor lock-in. The antitrust case against Microsoft set precedent for tech regulation. The wars ultimately led to the open standards web we have today.
